questions.sec: Superolateral temporal lobe and the auditory cortex
questions.q: How does the page open the superolateral temporal-lobe section, and which first row begins it?
opts: With a site-of-lesion and defect table whose first row covers the auditory cortex
With a homunculus of the medial limbic cortex
With a visual-field map of the occipital lobe only
With a Brodmann diagram of the parietal praxicon area
questions.exp: The superolateral temporal-lobe section opens with a site-of-lesion and defect table, and its opening row is the auditory cortex. (Book p563)

questions.sec: Superolateral temporal lobe and the auditory cortex
questions.q: Which Brodmann area pair is assigned to the auditory cortex?
opts: Areas 3, 1 and 2
Areas 41 and 42
Areas 44 and 45
Areas 17 and 18
questions.exp: The first table row labels the auditory cortex as areas 41 and 42. (Book p563)

questions.sec: Superolateral temporal lobe and the auditory cortex
questions.q: Which site-of-lesion entry does the page print for the auditory cortex?
opts: The medial occipital pole alone
The superior parietal lobule
Bilateral temporal lobe
Unilateral dominant frontal lobe
questions.exp: The table states that the auditory cortex occupies the bilateral temporal lobe, so its lesion is bilateral. (Book p563)

questions.sec: Superolateral temporal lobe and the auditory cortex
questions.q: What defect is paired with the auditory cortex in the table?
opts: Pure word deafness
Wernicke's aphasia with naming loss
Visual agnosia for objects
Deafness, described as auditory inattention
questions.exp: The defect column pairs the auditory cortex with deafness, parenthesised as auditory inattention. (Book p563)

questions.sec: Superolateral temporal lobe and the auditory cortex
questions.q: What do the auditory connection fibres link, and which defect follows their interruption?
opts: They run from the auditory cortex to Wernicke's area, and their interruption causes pure word deafness
They link Broca's area to the precentral gyrus, and interruption causes motor aphasia
They link the temporal lobe to the primary visual area, and interruption causes alexia
They link the thalamus to the mamillary body, and interruption causes confabulation
questions.exp: The auditory connection fibres join the auditory cortex to Wernicke's area, and their interruption is printed as causing pure word deafness. (Book p563)

questions.sec: Superolateral temporal lobe and the auditory cortex
questions.q: Which deficit is printed for a lesion of the auditory association cortex?
opts: Cortical blindness
Auditory agnosia
Visual agnosia
Ideomotor apraxia
questions.exp: The auditory association cortex row gives auditory agnosia as its defect. (Book p563)

questions.sec: Superolateral temporal lobe and the auditory cortex
questions.q: Which gyrus, area, deficit and spared function are all correctly paired for Wernicke's area?
opts: Middle temporal gyrus; area 21; visual neglect with weakness
Angular gyrus; area 39; alexia with agraphia and weakness
Superior temporal gyrus; area 22; Wernicke's aphasia affecting language comprehension, with no weakness
Inferior frontal gyrus; area 44; naming loss with contralateral hemiplegia
questions.exp: Wernicke's area is placed on the superior temporal gyrus and labelled area 22; its lesion gives Wernicke's aphasia, which is language comprehension, and no weakness. (Book p563)

questions.sec: Superolateral temporal lobe and the auditory cortex
questions.q: Which function and defect belong to the temporo-occipital association area?
opts: Language fluency, whose lesion causes non-fluent aphasia
Motor planning, whose lesion causes ideomotor apraxia
Memory consolidation, whose lesion causes Korsakoff's amnestic state
Visuospatial function, whose lesion causes visual agnosia: inability to identify objects by vision
questions.exp: The temporo-occipital association area is labelled for visuospatial function, and its defect is visual agnosia, defined as inability to identify objects by vision. (Book p563)

questions.sec: Superolateral temporal lobe and the auditory cortex
questions.q: Which hallucination set is attributed to lateral temporal lobe lesions?
opts: Auditory, olfactory and gustatory hallucinations
Visual, olfactory and vertiginous hallucinations
Gustatory and somatosensory hallucinations only
Auditory and visual hallucinations only
questions.exp: The page closes the lateral temporal-lobe list by attributing auditory, olfactory and gustatory hallucinations to lateral temporal lobe lesions. (Book p563)

questions.sec: Medial temporal lobe (limbic cortex) and its circuits
questions.q: Which heading and claim are printed for the medial temporal lobe?
opts: It is the primary auditory area and holds no limbic connections
It is the limbic cortex and is called the most epileptogenic focus in the body
It is the motor cortex and the least excitable region in the brain
It is the visual association area and cannot generate seizures
questions.exp: The heading MEDIAL TEMPORAL LOBE (LIMBIC CORTEX) is followed by the notice that it is the most epileptogenic focus in the body. (Book p563)

questions.sec: Medial temporal lobe (limbic cortex) and its circuits
questions.q: Which structures are labelled in the cingulate-cortex circuit diagram on this page?
opts: Superior parietal lobule, angular gyrus and the intraparietal sulcus
Calcarine sulcus, lingual gyrus and the cuneus only
Cingulate cortex, anterior thalamus, mamillary bodies and the medial temporal lobe
Precentral gyrus, postcentral gyrus and the pars opercularis
questions.exp: The cingulate-cortex figure joins the cingulate cortex to the anterior thalamus, mamillary bodies and the medial temporal lobe, the limbic loop. (Book p563)

questions.sec: Medial temporal lobe (limbic cortex) and its circuits
questions.q: Which labels belong to the cerebrum-components diagram rather than the loop diagram?
opts: Frontal eye field, Broca area and the orbital sulcus
Primary, peristriate and parastriate visual cortex
Vermis, flocculus and deep cerebellar nuclei
Cingulate gyrus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, fornix, hypothalamus, mammillary body and amygdaloid body
questions.exp: The components-in-the-cerebrum figure labels the cingulate gyrus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, corpus callosum, fornix, pineal gland, hypothalamus, mamillary body, anterior group of thalamic nuclei, amygdaloid body and caudate nucleus. (Book p563)

questions.sec: Components of the medial temporal lobe and their functions
questions.q: Which four components are listed for the medial temporal lobe?
opts: Superior temporal gyrus, inferior temporal gyrus, parahippocampus and fusiform gyrus
Precentral gyrus, postcentral gyrus, cingulate gyrus and precuneus
Rectus gyrus, olfactory sulcus, orbital sulcus and uncus
Calcarine sulcus, lingual gyrus, cuneus and splenium
questions.exp: The components column lists the superior temporal gyrus, inferior temporal gyrus, parahippocampus and fusiform gyrus as the medial temporal lobe parts. (Book p564)

questions.sec: Components of the medial temporal lobe and their functions
questions.q: Which five functions are listed for the medial temporal lobe?
opts: Posture, tone, gait, balance and coordination
Homeostasis, olfaction, memory, emotion and sexuality
Vision, audition, taste, proprioception and equilibrium
Fluency, comprehension, repetition, naming and reading
questions.exp: The functions column lists homeostasis, olfaction, memory, emotion and sexuality for the medial temporal lobe. (Book p564)

questions.sec: Components of the medial temporal lobe and their functions
questions.q: Which structure is the labelled medial temporal component in the coronal-section diagram?
opts: Fusiform gyrus
Superior temporal gyrus
Hippocampus
Amygdala
questions.exp: The coronal-section diagram in the cerebrum-components figure labels the hippocampus within the medial temporal region. (Book p564)

questions.sec: Components of the medial temporal lobe and their functions
questions.q: Which role and surface are printed together for the amygdala?
opts: It generates praxicons and lies on the superolateral surface
It produces speech and lies inside the inferior frontal gyrus
It stores visual memory and lies deep to the calcarine sulcus
It plays a role in memory and is present on the inferior surface
questions.exp: The page states the amygdala plays a role in memory and is present on the inferior surface. (Book p564)

questions.sec: Components of the medial temporal lobe and their functions
questions.q: What is the uncus described as?
opts: An elevation or bulge of the amygdala on the inferior surface
A sulcus separating the two motor homunculi
The posterior limit of the corpus callosum
A gyrus carrying the primary visual area
questions.exp: The uncus is described as the elevation or bulge of the amygdala on the inferior surface. (Book p564)

questions.sec: Components of the medial temporal lobe and their functions
questions.q: The page links herniation of the uncus to which clinical effect?
opts: It causes colour agnosia and dressing apraxia
It affects the pupil through a third-nerve palsy
It causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
It produces pure word deafness
questions.exp: Under the uncus, the note states that herniation affects the pupil, with third-nerve palsy given in parentheses. (Book p564)

questions.sec: Kluver-Bucy syndrome and Korsakoff's amnestic state
questions.q: Kluver-Bucy syndrome is described as also being (AKA) which combination?
opts: Bilateral basal-ganglia, thalamic and cerebellar abnormality
Unilateral temporal, hippocampal and mamillary-body abnormality
Bilateral limbic abnormality, bilateral medial temporal abnormality and bilateral amygdala abnormality
Unilateral frontal, parietal and occipital abnormality
questions.exp: The page writes Kluver-Bucy syndrome as AKA bilateral limbic abnormality, bilateral medial temporal abnormality and bilateral amygdala abnormality. (Book p564)

questions.sec: Kluver-Bucy syndrome and Korsakoff's amnestic state
questions.q: A patient with a bilateral limbic lesion is hypersexual. Which single feature of Kluver-Bucy syndrome is this?
opts: Hyperorality
Hypermetamorphosis
Visual agnosia
Hypersexuality
questions.exp: Hypersexuality is the first of the Kluver-Bucy features listed. (Book p564)

questions.sec: Kluver-Bucy syndrome and Korsakoff's amnestic state
questions.q: Which feature and its mechanism are correctly paired in the Kluver-Bucy list?
opts: Hyperorality, due to involvement of the hypothalamus, the feeding and satiety centre
Hyperorality, due to a frontal eye-field lesion
Hypermetamorphosis, due to superior-parietal praxicon loss
Hypersexuality, due to calcarine sulcus infarction
questions.exp: The page explains hyperorality as due to an affected hypothalamus, printing feeding and satiety centre in parentheses. (Book p564)

questions.sec: Kluver-Bucy syndrome and Korsakoff's amnestic state
questions.q: In Kluver-Bucy syndrome, visual agnosia is stated to affect which structures?
opts: The optic radiation only
Association areas
Primary auditory cortex
The anterior horn cell
questions.exp: The Kluver-Bucy visual-agnosia line states that it affects the association areas. (Book p564)

questions.sec: Kluver-Bucy syndrome and Korsakoff's amnestic state
questions.q: What is hypermetamorphosis explained as on the page?
opts: Overshoot of the finger on the finger-nose test
Inability to dress, such as putting on a jacket
Visual inattention: the need to touch any object to recognise it
The confabulation of visual descriptions in blindness
questions.exp: Hypermetamorphosis is printed as visual inattention, parenthesised as the need to touch any object to recognise it. (Book p564)

questions.sec: Kluver-Bucy syndrome and Korsakoff's amnestic state
questions.q: Which emotional change is listed in Kluver-Bucy syndrome?
opts: Increased fear and decreased aggression
Emotional lability with euphoria only
Apathy progressing to akinetic mutism
Decreased fear and increased aggression
questions.exp: The final Kluver-Bucy feature is decreased fear with increased aggression, printed as decreased Fear and increased Aggression. (Book p564)

questions.sec: Kluver-Bucy syndrome and Korsakoff's amnestic state
questions.q: Which two findings together account for Korsakoff's amnestic state on this page?
opts: A bilateral temporal lobe lesion and abnormality in the mamillary body
A unilateral parietal lesion and an intact hippocampus
A frontal eye-field lesion and a normal fornix
A bilateral occipital infarct and splenium involvement
questions.exp: Korsakoff's amnestic state is printed as due to a bilateral temporal lobe lesion with abnormality in the mamillary body. (Book p564)

questions.sec: Apathy, occipital lesions and Balint's syndrome
questions.q: Apathy is attributed by the page to lesions of which two sites?
opts: The superior temporal gyrus and auditory cortex
The medial prefrontal cortex and thalamic connections
The medial temporal lobe and mamillary body
The superior parietal lobule and angular gyrus
questions.exp: The apathy note states that the lesion is in the medial prefrontal cortex and the thalamic connections. (Book p565)

questions.sec: Apathy, occipital lesions and Balint's syndrome
questions.q: Which defect is printed for a lesion of the primary visual area (area 17)?
opts: Superior homonymous quadrantanopia called pie in the sky
Inferior homonymous quadrantanopia called pie in the floor
Contralateral congruent homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
Bilateral cortical blindness with confabulation
questions.exp: The unilateral-lesion column gives the primary visual area (17) a contralateral congruent homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. (Book p565)

questions.sec: Apathy, occipital lesions and Balint's syndrome
questions.q: Which areas form the visual association area, and what cortex do they represent?
opts: Areas 17 and 18, the primary and premotor cortex
Areas 41 and 42, the parasitic auditory cortex
Areas 44 and 45, the peri-arcuate speech cortex
Areas 18 and 19, the parastriate and peristriate cortex
questions.exp: The visual association area is printed as areas 18 and 19, labelled parastriate and peristriate cortex. (Book p565)

questions.sec: Apathy, occipital lesions and Balint's syndrome
questions.q: Which functions are listed for the visual association area?
opts: Ocular fixation, fixing size, shape and colour, and visual memory
Hearing, balance, taste and smell
Fluency, comprehension, repetition and naming
Posture, gait, tone and coordination
questions.exp: The functions listed under the visual association area are ocular fixation, fixing size/shape/colour and visual memory. (Book p565)

questions.sec: Apathy, occipital lesions and Balint's syndrome
questions.q: A lesion of the visual association area produces which deficit?
opts: Gerstmann syndrome
Colour agnosia
Cerebral achromatopsia
Pure word deafness
questions.exp: The visual association area's defect line reads lesion → colour agnosia. (Book p565)

questions.sec: Apathy, occipital lesions and Balint's syndrome
questions.q: Which labels are placed in the medial-view diagram around the primary visual area?
opts: The precentral gyrus and the central sulcus labelled area 4
The angular gyrus and the intraparietal sulcus labelled area 39
The calcarine sulcus, the parieto-occipital fissure and the primary visual area labelled area 17
The auditory cortex and the Sylvian fissure labelled area 41
questions.exp: The medial-view drawing labels the calcarine sulcus, the parieto-occipital fissure, the sagittal sulci, the lingual and cingulate landmarks and the primary visual area as area 17. (Book p565)

questions.sec: Apathy, occipital lesions and Balint's syndrome
questions.q: Which vision state is described in Anton's syndrome?
opts: Contralateral hemianopia with full insight and accurate reporting
Inability to identify objects by vision despite intact fields
Overshoot of the finger on the finger-nose test
Cortical blindness with unawareness of blindness: the patient confabulates visual descriptions or blames poor vision on dim light or missing spectacles
questions.exp: Anton's syndrome describes cortical blindness without awareness of it; the patient confabulates a visual description or blames dim light or missing spectacles. (Book p565)

questions.sec: Apathy, occipital lesions and Balint's syndrome
questions.q: What happens to the light reflex in Anton's syndrome?
opts: It remains intact
It is lost bilaterally
It shows an afferent pupillary defect
It becomes sluggish on the blind side only
questions.exp: The Anton's syndrome note ends with the statement that the light reflex is intact. (Book p565)

questions.sec: Apathy, occipital lesions and Balint's syndrome
questions.q: Which two colour-vision deficits are listed after Anton's syndrome?
opts: Xanthopsia and erythropsia
Colour agnosia and cerebral achromatopsia
Colour agnosia and dyschromatopsia of rods only
Achromatopsia and oscillopsia
questions.exp: The two printed colour-vision deficits are colour agnosia and cerebral achromatopsia. (Book p565)

questions.sec: Apathy, occipital lesions and Balint's syndrome
questions.q: In Balint's syndrome, optic ataxia is clarified as which finding?
opts: Unawareness of blindness with confabulation
Loss of orientation to familiar places
Gauge abnormality: overshoot on the finger-nose test
Inability to name a seen object
questions.exp: Optic ataxia in Balint's syndrome is parenthesised as gauge abnormality, with overshoot on the finger-nose test. (Book p565)

questions.sec: Apathy, occipital lesions and Balint's syndrome
questions.q: Which two components accompany optic ataxia in Balint's syndrome?
opts: Dressing apraxia and constructional apraxia
Ideational apraxia and ideomotor apraxia
Prosopagnosia and alexia without agraphia
Oculomotor apraxia and simultanagnosia, perceiving only specific details at a time rather than the whole
questions.exp: Balint's syndrome lists optic ataxia plus oculomotor apraxia and simultanagnosia, the last described as perceiving only specific details at a time rather than the whole. (Book p565)

questions.sec: Apathy, occipital lesions and Balint's syndrome
questions.q: Which lesion produces Balint's syndrome on this page?
opts: A bilateral occipital lobe lesion
A unilateral dominant parietal lobe lesion
A lateral temporal lobe lesion
A medial prefrontal cortex lesion
questions.exp: Balint's syndrome is attributed to a bilateral occipital lobe lesion in the B/L-lesion column. (Book p565)

units.title: 1. Superolateral temporal lobe and the auditory cortex
units.sec: Superolateral temporal lobe and the auditory cortex
units.guide:
The page opens with a site-of-lesion and defect table for the superolateral temporal lobe.
The auditory cortex, its connection fibres and the temporo-occipital association area are kept in printed order.

units.title: 2. Medial temporal lobe (limbic cortex) and its circuits
units.sec: Medial temporal lobe (limbic cortex) and its circuits
units.guide:
The medial temporal lobe (limbic cortex) note and its limbic diagrams are read after the lateral list.
Cingulate, thalamic, mamillary, hippocampal and amygdala labels form the limbic circuit on this page.

units.title: 3. Components of the medial temporal lobe and their functions
units.sec: Components of the medial temporal lobe and their functions
units.guide:
The components and functions columns are read in sequence, then the coronal-section diagram and the amygdala/uncus notes (including herniation's third-nerve palsy).
See the coronal section for the hippocampus label and the inferior surface for the amygdala bulge.

units.title: 4. Kluver-Bucy syndrome and Korsakoff's amnestic state
units.sec: Kluver-Bucy syndrome and Korsakoff's amnestic state
units.guide:
The Kluver-Bucy equivalence and its five features are read in order, then the bilateral temporal Korsakoff's amnestic-state note closes the page.
Hypersexuality, hyperorality, visual agnosia, hypermetamorphosis and the emotional change are kept in the printed sequence.

units.title: 5. Apathy, occipital lesions and Balint's syndrome
units.sec: Apathy, occipital lesions and Balint's syndrome
units.guide:
The apathy note leads into the occipital lobe: the W/L (unilateral) and B/L lesion columns, the medial-view visual-area diagram, the colour-deficit list and Balint's syndrome, all in printed order.
The primary visual area, the visual association area, Anton's syndrome and the colour deficits lead into the bilateral-lesion Balint's trio.
